tagline: A river passage links old trading paths, rock walls and Marshall.
intro: The French Broad Overview follows the river between Marshall and Weaverville, with sheer rock walls marking the passage cut through the valley. North Carolina’s scenic-byway program includes this 16.3-mile drive; NCDOT highlights its river recreation, palisades and trading-path history. The river once carried goods and now draws canoeists, tubers and rafters in summer. NCDOT gives the drive a 30-minute travel time. Marshall’s riverbank setting is tightly confined: the French Broad bounds one side of the townsite, and steep mountain terrain surrounds the other sides.

The road developed along Native American trading paths leading toward posts and villages in the Tennessee and Ohio River valleys. European settlers followed those established passages and widened the paths into roads. Railways subsequently used the same advantage of the river valleys.

Traveling from the Marshall end, begin where Main Street meets the US 25/70 bypass and follow Main Street through town toward the Ivey River crossing. NC 251, the Old Marshall Highway, carries the route along the river past Alexander. Monticello Road completes the journey to US 25/70 in Weaverville. The Vance Birthplace in the Reems Creek Valley is a separate excursion from this end of the drive.
notice: Look for the sheer rock walls beside the river road, where the French Broad cut into the valley sides.

moments.title: Marshall
moments.text: The French Broad River bounds one side of Marshall; steep mountain terrain confines the others. Main Street carries US 70 Business through town, while US 25 and US 70 bypass it to the northeast. The county seat’s courthouse was built in 1907 to a design by Smith & Carrier, with a polygonal cupola above its hipped roof. The river setting also carries a recent history of destruction: Hurricane Helene damaged the town hall and destroyed several buildings in 2024. The Main Street historic district entered the National Register of Historic Places in 2007.

moments.title: Weaverville
moments.text: A Methodist meeting place became an early school in Weaverville. The conference house, built in the 1830s on the Reems Creek Camp Grounds, took on its educational role in 1840. Weaverville College followed with a charter in 1873, later becoming a junior college and merging with Rutherford and Brevard Colleges in 1934. The town’s Methodist church was built in 1919–1920, with a two-story front portico and a later educational building added in 1956–1957. The town was chartered in 1875 and named for Michael Montraville Weaver, who supplied the land for it.

moments.title: Vance Birthplace
moments.text: Eighteen enslaved people lived and worked on the Vance farm in the Reems Creek Valley. David Vance II and Mira Margaret Baird Vance owned this mountain plantation, where Zebulon Baird Vance was born in 1830. He later served as North Carolina’s Civil War governor. The state historic site includes a loom house, tool shed, spring house, smoke house and corn crib. The Vance home is a reconstruction of the 1790s house; the site also interprets a 1790 slave house and the lives of the people enslaved on the farm. The North Carolina Division of State Historic Sites owns and operates the property.
